content: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a progressive and debilitating muscle disorder that begins in childhood and leads to severe physical disability and a reduced life expectancy. The condition arises from a profound deficiency of dystrophin, a protein that plays critical structural and signaling roles in both skeletal and cardiac muscle cells. In DMD, calcium accumulates abnormally within muscle cells, contributing to cellular damage. It has been hypothesized that calcium antagonists, which are drugs designed to block calcium influx, might mitigate this calcium overload and its toxic effects on muscle cells. The objective of this review was to assess the impact of calcium antagonists on muscle strength and function in individuals with DMD. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Trials Register, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies published up to July 2010. The review also included an examination of bibliographies from relevant trial reports. The inclusion criteria were limited to randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving any calcium antagonist in individuals diagnosed with DMD. Two authors independently evaluated all identified trials to determine their eligibility based on the selection criteria. They also extracted data and assessed the methodological quality of the studies. If multiple trials of the same intervention and outcome had been available and met sufficient methodological standards, a meta-analysis was planned. However, this was not possible due to the heterogeneity of the studies. Five randomized or quasi-randomized double-blind trials met the inclusion criteria. These trials investigated the effects of the calcium antagonists verapamil (8 participants), diltiazem (56 participants), nifedipine (105 participants), and flunarizine (27 participants). However, the trials were not sufficiently comparable to allow for a meta-analysis. Methodological limitations were noted, including inadequate descriptions of blinding and randomization processes, as well as poorly defined outcome measures. One trial involving verapamil demonstrated a difference in muscle force, as measured by ergometry, between the treatment and control groups. However, this trial also reported cardiac side effects associated with verapamil use. Across all studies, the sample sizes were small, which limited the statistical power to detect subtle differences in muscle strength or function between the treatment and placebo groups. Furthermore, the calcium antagonists studied were in the early stages of development, and newer-generation drugs with improved side effect profiles, such as amlodipine, were not included in these trials. In conclusion, there is currently no evidence to support a significant beneficial effect of calcium antagonists on muscle function in individuals with DMD.
